question: Law of giving effect to fundamental rights can only be made by the ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliament**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In India, the power to enact laws for giving effect to fundamental rights resides with the **Parliament under Article 35 of the Constitution**.
 
• Article 35 specifies that only Parliament can make laws to enforce certain provisions in Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution.
 
• This provision ensures **uniformity in laws related to fundamental rights across the country**, preventing variations among states.
 
• For example, laws related to punitive measures for offenses under Article 17 (Abolition of Untouchability) or Article 23 (Prohibition of Traffic in Human Beings and Forced Labour) are made exclusively by the Parliament.
 
• The intent of reserving this power for Parliament is to safeguard the supremacy of the Constitution and the integrity of fundamental rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights**

 
 
• These are a set of rights enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, ensuring equality, freedom, and justice for all citizens.
 
• The six categories of fundamental rights include Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• They are enforceable by courts, and citizens can approach the judiciary for violations under Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies).
 
 
 
• **Article 35: Key Features**
 
 
• Article 35 empowers only the Parliament to make laws for implementing certain Fundamental Rights, such as laws against untouchability and human trafficking.
 
• It also restricts state legislatures from creating laws on specific matters related to fundamental rights.
 
 
 
• **Role of Judiciary**
 
 
• The judiciary, particularly the Supreme Court, plays a critical role in safeguarding fundamental rights by interpreting laws and striking down unconstitutional provisions.
 
• However, it does not have the legislative power to enact laws—it can only adjudicate upon them.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary Supremacy in Law-Making**
 
 
• Parliament is the supreme legislative body in India, with the power to make laws for the entire country under the Union List and Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule.
 
• Its role in enforcing fundamental rights underscores its central position in the democratic framework.
